title: A night of sleep
subtitle: The brain does not switch off — it switches mode
question: What happens in your brain while you sleep?
teaser: Squeeze eight hours into one dial and watch your brain change mode.
intro: Sleep is not your brain switching off. It is a sequence of different modes, each with its own pattern of activity, cycling several times a night. Memory, cleaning up, and how well you think the next day all depend on that sequence actually happening.

events.title: Awake
events.explanation: Systems deep in your brain hold the central gate open. Information flows, your brain responds to it, and you can form memories of what happens.

events.title: The switch flips
events.explanation: Circuitry at the base tips the balance. This is closer to a switch flipping than a gradual fade.
events.science: Sleep–wake switching circuits are mutually inhibitory, which makes the transition relatively fast and the intermediate states unstable.

events.title: N1 — the threshold
events.explanation: Alertness drops. Thoughts get fragmentary, muscles relax, and you may not be sure whether you were asleep.

events.title: The gate begins to close
events.explanation: The gate starts closing. Sound still reaches you — it just stops spreading through the brain. That is why a noise can register and not wake you.
events.science: This is why a sound can be loud enough to register and still not wake you. The input is not blocked at the ear.

events.title: N2 — spindles and bursts
events.explanation: Short bursts of coordinated activity appear. How many you get relates to how well you hold on to things you learned that day.
events.science: Spindle density correlates with overnight retention of recently learned material. The relationship is robust, though its causal interpretation is still being worked out.

events.title: Reactivation begins
events.explanation: Patterns from your day get replayed in bursts, with nothing happening to trigger them.

events.title: N3 — deep sleep
events.explanation: Huge numbers of cells switch between active and silent almost in unison. This is the most synchronised your brain ever gets.
events.science: Slow-wave activity is deepest early in the night and is associated with restorative processes and with the consolidation of recent declarative material.

events.title: Coordinated consolidation
events.explanation: The replay, the bursts and the slow rhythm line up in time with each other. The lining-up itself seems to be the part that matters.
events.science: Experimentally enhancing or disrupting the coupling between these rhythms changes overnight retention, which is some of the strongest evidence that sleep does memory work rather than merely coinciding with it.

events.title: Into REM
events.explanation: Another switch. Your brain starts looking much more like it does awake, while your muscles are actively held still.

events.title: REM — vivid, internally generated experience
events.explanation: Seeing and feeling systems are very busy. The parts that hold goals and check whether things make sense are much less so — which fits how dreams go.
events.science: Dreaming is not exclusive to REM and REM is not purely dreaming. The correlation is strong and the identity is not.

events.title: The body is held still
events.explanation: Signals going down keep your muscles still so you do not act out what is happening. When that fails, people really do act out their dreams.

events.title: Emotional processing
events.explanation: Emotional systems are active while the parts that usually damp them down are quiet. This phase seems to help process the day's feelings.

events.title: And the cycle repeats
events.explanation: And round again, roughly every ninety minutes, four to six times a night. The mix shifts: deep sleep early, dreaming sleep toward morning.
events.science: This is why sleeping four hours is not half a night's sleep. The two halves of the night are doing different work.

causalChain.label: Wake is actively maintained
causalChain.detail: Staying awake is something your brain actively does, not a default.

causalChain.label: A switch flips
causalChain.detail: A switch flips, quickly rather than gradually.

causalChain.label: Transmission mode changes
causalChain.detail: Sound still arrives but stops spreading.

causalChain.label: Coordinated bursts appear
causalChain.detail: Bursts of activity appear, tied to holding on to what you learned.

causalChain.label: Deep synchronisation
causalChain.detail: Huge numbers of cells start switching on and off together.

causalChain.label: Rhythms couple
causalChain.detail: Replay, bursts and slow rhythm line up in time.

causalChain.label: REM begins
causalChain.detail: Your brain goes wake-like while your muscles are held still.

causalChain.label: Internally generated experience
causalChain.detail: Vivid experience is generated with nothing coming in from outside.

science.text: Sleep consists of distinct, identifiable global states that cycle several times per night with a period of roughly ninety minutes.
Deep slow-wave sleep predominates in the first half of the night and REM in the second.
Most skeletal muscle is actively inhibited during REM sleep; failure of this inhibition is a recognised clinical disorder.
Experimentally disrupting sleep after learning impairs retention, and enhancing specific sleep rhythms can improve it.
We show one clean cycle. A real night is irregular, with varying stage durations, brief awakenings and considerable individual variation.
The circular timeline compresses roughly eight hours into fourteen seconds. The proportions are representative of a typical night, not of any particular one.

This is not an EEG simulator. The waveform drawn on the dial is a stylised illustration of how synchronisation changes between states — it is not generated from a model of cortical electrical activity, and it is not anyone's recording.
Nothing here is sleep-tracking or health advice. Sleep varies enormously between people and across the lifespan.

references.label: Sleep staging
references.note: The standard classification of sleep into N1, N2, N3 and REM, based on characteristic electrophysiological signatures.

references.label: Sleep-dependent consolidation
references.note: Evidence that sleep after learning benefits retention, with different stages implicated in different kinds of material.

references.label: Flip-flop switch model
references.note: An account of sleep–wake transitions as mutually inhibitory circuits producing fast state changes.

references.label: Rhythm coupling
references.note: Work on the temporal nesting of hippocampal reactivation, thalamocortical spindles and cortical slow oscillations.

outcome.headline: Sleeping
outcome.body: The gate opened and closed, your brain moved through several different modes, the day's experiences were replayed and made more stable, and a wake-like phase generated vivid experience while your body stayed completely still.
outcome.insight: None of this is downtime. The sequence does work that cannot be done while you are awake — and the second half of the night does a different job from the first.
